fields.title: Nerpa: paying per user, but using it differently
fields.summary: The pricing metric no longer aligns with value. Decide how to restructure the model.
fields.decisionPrompt: What will you do with the monetization model?
fields.brief/role: You are the product manager of Nerpa.
fields.brief/company: Nerpa is a fictional ticket tracking service for service centers: 430 clients, pricing of 900 ₽ per user per month.
fields.brief/context: Revenue has been flat for three quarters despite client growth. It turns out that clients create one shared account per shift to avoid paying for each technician. The board suggests blocking this technically.
fields.brief/objective: Decide what to do with the monetization model.
fields.brief/constraints: Six months until annual planning. Cash runway — 14 months.
fields.brief/task: Choose a solution and justify it.
fields.learnTakeaway/title: Customers bypass a poor metric, not the rules
fields.learnTakeaway/body: When they pay for one thing but use another, workarounds appear naturally and cannot be cured by bans — they are cured by changing what you charge for. A good pricing metric grows alongside customer value and your variable costs; then the customer has no reason to argue with it. And it's better to transition them to it as contracts expire, not by decree.
fields.evidenceCards/0/content:
430 clients, average of 2.4 paid users per client.

According to login data: in 61% of clients, at least three different people work under one account — different devices, overlapping times.

Average number of tickets processed by a client per month: from 40 for small ones to 3,000 for large ones. The payment is almost the same.

The largest client processes 3,000 tickets per month and pays for three users — 2,700 ₽.

Infrastructure load grows with the number of tickets, not users: variable costs for large clients are four times higher than for small ones, with the same revenue.

Contribution by segment: small — positive; large by tickets — close to zero or negative.
fields.evidenceCards/1/content:
In 16 interviews, the same thing is repeated: the value is that no ticket is lost and it's clear what stage it is at.

Value grows with the number of tickets: those with 40 a month 'could just use a notebook'; those with 3,000 cannot work without the product.

No one mentions the number of users as a value.

Clients do not consider a shared account to be cheating: 'technicians work in shifts anyway, why pay for each one'.

At the same time, a shared account breaks part of the product: it's unclear who took the ticket, there is no history by technician, and analytics is impossible — which is exactly what two dozen clients are asking to pay extra for.

When asked about pricing per ticket, the reaction is calm: 'that's fair, we pay for what we use'.
fields.evidenceCards/2/content:
Board: technically block shared accounts — device binding, idle timeout.

CCO: raise the price per user from 900 to 1,400 ₽.

One of the PMs: change the pricing metric to the number of tickets.

CFO: any price change for existing clients is a churn risk, currently it is 7% per year.

Transition to the new metric: 6 weeks of development plus a month to recalculate contracts.

Two competitors charge per user; one charges per ticket, and they grew twofold over the year.
fields.evidenceCards/3/content:
When switching to pay-per-ticket, 30% of small clients will see their payment decrease, while 12% of large ones will see it increase by 3–6 times.

According to calculations, total revenue when moving everyone to the new model will grow by about 40%, but the distribution will change significantly.

Active contracts are annual, renewed as they expire throughout the year.

Blocking shared accounts, based on the experience of two similar companies, causes a spike in churn: people perceive it as a downgrade without any new value.

Analytics by technician is requested by 22 clients — it is only possible with personal accounts.

Runway is 14 months, burn rate is moderate: there is time for a careful transition.
fields.decisionOptions/0/description: Tie payment to what grows alongside value and our costs, transition gradually as contracts expire, and provide personal accounts for free.
fields.decisionOptions/0/consequence:
The metric starts to align with three things at once: customer value (no tickets are lost), our variable costs (load grows from tickets), and willingness to pay — in interviews, the reaction to pay-per-ticket is calm.
You make personal accounts free, and the shared account disappears on its own: there is no longer a need to pay for users, and the analytics by technician requested by 22 clients requires personal accounts.
You transition them as annual contracts expire — over a year without a single forced renegotiation.
The largest client with 3,000 tickets switches from 2,700 ₽ to a significantly larger amount; for 30% of small clients, the payment decreases, and they are happy about it.
Over the year, revenue grows by 34%, churn remains at 7%.
Trade-off: one and a half months of development and contract recalculation, and some large clients had difficult negotiations about the transition period.
fields.decisionOptions/1/description: The board is right: clients bypass the tariff. Bind the account to the device and log out on inactivity.
fields.decisionOptions/1/consequence:
Technically this works: the number of paid users grows from 2.4 to 3.6 per client in a quarter.
But clients perceive this as a downgrade without any new value — exactly like two similar cases in the market. Churn grows from 7% to 15% over the year.
Some clients leave for a competitor that charges per ticket: their expenses turn out to be lower there.
At the same time, the discrepancy between what they pay for and where our costs come from remains: large clients by tickets still bring a negative contribution.
Trade-off: workaround behavior is stopped, but its cause — the wrong pricing metric — is preserved; clients paid for this by leaving.
fields.decisionOptions/2/description: 900 ₽ is too low. Raise it to 1,400 ₽ and get the required revenue without changing the model.
fields.decisionOptions/2/consequence:
The increase strengthens the motive to share accounts: the more expensive the user, the more profitable it is to share one.
Over the quarter, the average number of paid users drops from 2.4 to 2.0, and revenue grows by only 4% instead of the calculated 55%.
Large clients, who generate the main infrastructure load, still pay for two or three users.
Churn rises to 9% — some small clients leave, as the product was already on the edge for them.
Trade-off: the price was raised on a metric that the client knows how to evade, so the increase was paid by those who did not evade it.
fields.decisionOptions/3/label: Sell analytics as a separate module
fields.decisionOptions/3/description: Analytics by technician is requested by 22 clients, and it requires personal accounts. Make it paid — then clients will create accounts themselves.
fields.decisionOptions/3/consequence:
An elegant move: analytics is sold to 19 out of 22 clients, and they indeed create personal accounts to make it work.
Revenue grows by 6%, churn remains unchanged — this is a neat solution without conflict.
But the scale is wrong: 22 clients out of 430, while the discrepancy between the pricing metric and the load remains for everyone else.
The largest client with 3,000 tickets still pays 2,700 ₽.
Six months later, the question returns in the exact same form.
Trade-off: a good local measure taken instead of a model decision; however, it honestly proves that clients do not mind personal accounts in themselves.
fields.rubric/remediation/0/gap: Economics are calculated for the whole company, not per customer and by segment
fields.rubric/remediation/1/gap: The decision was made without considering reserves, burn rate, and runway
